title: Chemistry index + often-missed redflags (quick passback)
body:
Quick sketch for myself after loop with candidate (backend/runtime). Goal: capture soft chemistry signals + concrete blockers that often get missed in normal scorecards. Use before final vote and during onboarding-risk calibration.

High-level impression:
- Technical baseline: solid systems fundamentals, strong on memory/kv cache reasoning, pragmatic about tradeoffs. Not super deep on CUDA/kernels (flag).
- Communication: concise, interrupts a bit when excited — sometimes skips clarifying questions. Good at diagrams once prompted.
- Ops instincts: good SRE empathy, named concrete runbook ideas (nice).

Immediate redflags (probation / onboarding risk):
- CUDA/low-level GPU experience: candidate's experience = research-adjacent/CPU heavy. If role expects shipping kernel patches in first 6 months, that'll be a ramp risk.
- Ownership framing: tends to propose engineering-by-prototype; may under-index on long-term maintainability unless paired with strong tech lead.
- Silent assumption pattern: made several assumptions about data distribution (token length) without asking product/metrics. Could cause model-config regressions in prod.

Soft signals (could go either way):
- Curious but bounded: asks follow-ups after I press; will hunt for answers but may need prompts to verify assumptions.
- Pragmatic tradeoffs: prefers simple, measurable fixes (caching, batching) vs big architectural rewrites. Good for rapid iteration teams.

Concrete examples from loop:
- On KV cache question, suggested an LRU+prefix-shared cache that would shave ~8-12% token work — idea reasonable, but didn't surface eviction complexity for multi-tenant SLOs.
- When asked about model fallbacks, offered region-fallback + smaller model combo; missed data privacy implication (VPC routing) until I asked.
- Implementation vignette: wrote pseudocode for continuous batching but used naive lock granularity — we flagged for lock contention at scale.

Questions to cover in follow-up (if we do a second loop or hiring manager sync):
- Depth in GPU performance debugging: specific kernel-level debugging examples, perf counters used, concrete flamegraph/trace interpretation.
- Ownership story: a time they refactored a long-lived system; tradeoffs and how they measured risk.
- Multi-tenant caching: how they'd handle eviction across customers with different SLAs.

Quick score heuristics (for my internal use):
- Tech depth (systems/inference): 7/10 (strip for CUDA)
- Production ownership: 6/10
- Culture fit / collaboration: 8/10
- Ramp risk (first 3 months): medium-high if kernel work required

Recommendation direction (draft):
- Good candidate for teams focusing on integration-level inference improvements (batching, caching, routing).
- Not a green-light for roles that require immediate kernel/kernel-level perf ownership; would need 3-6 months pairing with a senior infra/kernel engineer.
- If hiring committee wants broader applicability, ask for an optional take-home or short pairing session focused on a perf debugging vignette (30–45 min) to validate kernel/trace fluency.

Next actions (my TODO):
- Ping hiring manager (Maya) with this passback + ask if kernel ownership is a hard requirement for the role.
- If still interested, propose a focused pairing session next week; draft prompt: "Given a 2x token latency regression after quantization, debug plan + 30m pairing on perf counters."
- Add flagged follow-ups to JIRA-IR-412 and share this note in hiring thread (slack).

Notes to self: keep this succinct for committee — focus on ramp risks and concrete examples. Leave ambiguity on cultural fit for others to weigh in.

End of passback.
